name: Procrastination Type Test
tagline: Find out why you put things off and how to start.
intro: Everyone procrastinates, but not for the same reason. This test compares five common procrastination styles: the perfectionist, the avoider, the thrill seeker, the overwhelmed and the distracted. Rate how much you agree with each statement. It takes about five minutes and shows your main style, with concrete strategies that fit how you work.
seoTitle: Procrastination Type Test – Find your style
seoDescription: Why do you procrastinate? Take this free 5-minute test to discover your procrastination type and get concrete strategies that fit the way you work.

perfectionist.name: The Perfectionist
perfectionist.short: Delaying because the result has to be flawless.
perfectionist.low: Your answers suggest perfectionism rarely holds you back. You seem able to start before everything is perfect and to accept good-enough results when time is short. This flexibility helps you finish things. On tasks that truly matter, such as a key presentation, it can still be worth planning a short extra round of review, so quality does not slip where it counts.
perfectionist.mid: Your answers suggest perfectionism sometimes slows you down, especially on tasks that will be judged by others. High standards are valuable, but they can make starting feel heavy. Try a deliberately rough first draft: give yourself permission to write badly for twenty minutes. Decide in advance what done looks like, for example three clear points or one review round, and stop when you reach it.
perfectionist.high: Your answers suggest perfectionism is a major reason you procrastinate. When a task has to be flawless, starting feels risky and finishing feels impossible, so you delay or keep polishing. Strategies that help: set a strict time box for each phase, aim for a version one rather than a final version, and share early drafts with one trusted person. Ask yourself what would be good enough for this purpose. If fear of failure causes ongoing stress or low mood, a qualified professional can help.

avoider.name: The Avoider
avoider.short: Delaying tasks that feel unpleasant, boring or uncomfortable.
avoider.low: Your answers suggest you usually face unpleasant tasks without much delay. Awkward emails, dull paperwork or difficult calls do not seem to pile up for long. This saves you the stress of having them hang over you. Keep using what works, such as doing the worst task first or pairing it with something you enjoy, and notice if new kinds of tasks start to slip.
avoider.mid: Your answers suggest you sometimes put off tasks because they feel unpleasant or uncomfortable. The relief of delaying is real, but it is short-lived. Try the two-minute start: commit to working on the task for only two minutes, then decide whether to continue. Pairing a dull task with music, a nice drink or a reward afterwards can also make it easier to begin.
avoider.high: Your answers suggest avoiding unpleasant feelings is a main driver of your procrastination. Tasks that feel boring, awkward or threatening get pushed aside, which brings quick relief but often more stress later. Name the feeling the task brings up, such as dread or boredom, and remind yourself that it usually fades once you start. Schedule unpleasant tasks early in the day and make the first step tiny. If avoidance is linked to strong anxiety or low mood, consider talking to a qualified professional.

thrill_seeker.name: The Thrill Seeker
thrill_seeker.short: Delaying until the pressure of a deadline kicks in.
thrill_seeker.low: Your answers suggest you do not rely on deadline pressure to get going. You seem to start tasks early and work at a steady pace, which reduces stress and leaves room for surprises. Keep this habit, and occasionally use a short, self-set sprint to add energy when a task feels dull, without letting it turn into last-minute rushing. Your calm pace is also a good example for others.
thrill_seeker.mid: Your answers suggest you sometimes wait for a deadline to get motivated. Pressure can give you focus, but it also leaves little room for mistakes or unexpected problems. Create your own earlier deadlines and make them real, for instance by promising a draft to a colleague. Break big projects into several mini-deadlines so you get the energy of urgency more than once.
thrill_seeker.high: Your answers suggest you strongly rely on last-minute pressure to get things done. The adrenaline can feel productive, but it often costs sleep, quality and peace of mind, and one surprise can derail everything. Use the urgency you like in a smarter way: set artificial deadlines with real consequences, work in timed sprints and tell someone when you will deliver. Track how long tasks actually take. If constant rushing affects your health or sleep, consider speaking with a qualified professional.

overwhelmed.name: The Overwhelmed
overwhelmed.short: Delaying because tasks feel too big, too many or unclear.
overwhelmed.low: Your answers suggest you rarely freeze when work piles up. You seem able to see where to start and to break larger tasks into steps. This is a valuable skill for busy periods. Keep supporting it with a simple planning routine, such as a short daily list of your top three priorities, so it holds up even under heavy pressure.
overwhelmed.mid: Your answers suggest you sometimes get stuck when tasks feel big or numerous. In those moments, procrastination is less about laziness and more about not knowing where to begin. Write down every task, then choose just one and define its very first physical step, such as opening the file. Limit your daily list to three priorities and celebrate finishing them.
overwhelmed.high: Your answers suggest that feeling overwhelmed is a main reason you procrastinate. When everything seems big, unclear or urgent at once, freezing is a natural reaction. Start by emptying your head onto paper, then choose one small, concrete next step. Ask for clarification when instructions are vague, and say no to new commitments where you can. Rest also matters: tired minds stall more easily. If overwhelm feels constant or affects your wellbeing, please consider talking to a doctor or a qualified professional.

distracted.name: The Distracted
distracted.short: Delaying because attention drifts to other things.
distracted.low: Your answers suggest you can usually stay focused and resist distractions. Phones, notifications and interesting side paths do not seem to pull you off course for long. This makes your working time efficient. Protect this strength by keeping your workspace calm and planning short breaks, so your focus stays fresh across a long day. Doing your most demanding work at your sharpest time of day helps even more.
distracted.mid: Your answers suggest distractions sometimes get between you and your tasks. You can focus, but your phone, browser or surroundings regularly break your attention. Try working in fixed blocks of twenty-five to fifty minutes with notifications off and your phone in another room. Keep a notepad nearby to jot down stray ideas so you can return to them later instead of acting on them right away.
distracted.high: Your answers suggest distraction is a main cause of your procrastination. Your attention may jump between tasks, screens and ideas, leaving important work unfinished. Change your environment rather than relying on willpower: use website blockers, silence notifications and work somewhere with fewer interruptions. Start each block with one clearly defined task. Body doubling, working alongside someone else, can help too. If attention problems are persistent and affect your work or wellbeing, a qualified professional can help you explore what lies behind them.

summary: Your main procrastination type is the style that scored highest, but most people show a mix of several. Below you see how strongly each style appears in your answers, with an explanation and strategies. Higher scores mean that style plays a bigger role for you. This is a self-reflection tool, not a diagnosis.
